items.title: Non-Coders Built a Video Game on Day 1
items.summary: In episode 1039 of the SuperDataScience Podcast, Jon Krohn talks with Dr. John Renne about teaching AI to real estate students at Tulane University who have almost no coding experience. Dr. Renne describes students building a video game the very first time they opened a vibe coding app, using material from Ed Donner's Udemy course, then moving on to Kanban boards, personal websites and a final project: a tool to help the public understand their real estate assessments.

items.title: Anthropic is Hiring Less Junior Tech Workers?
items.summary: The grunt work that taught me how to do my job is the same work Anthropic says its teams can now hand to Claude. Anthropic studied its own hiring. The junior share of its technical hires fell from 27% to 9%, and that happened while the company kept hiring. The teams that use Claude most said a lot of coding and bug finding can move to the AI. When interviewers wrote up candidates, comments about judgment and working independently grew more than anything else. When I started at Scouts, I had very little to show for myself. For the first year, I mostly wrote code, put together slide decks, did basic analysis, and tried to build trust with our clients. None of it felt like training at the time. Looking back, that year is where I learned what clients care about and how to explain a finding so someone believes it. The judgment companies now screen for came out of that work. I didn’t walk in with it. I’m not directly on the hiring side, but over the last five years I’ve helped sports teams interview and hire a fair amount. I understand the pull. If AI can handle the first draft, it makes sense to hire people who already know what to do with it. I just don’t know who trains the next group if every organization makes that call. One caveat: this is one company studying itself, and it sells the tool, so it may not predict what every employer does. Still, it’s worth paying attention to. If you’re early in your career, the reps that used to come with a first job won’t show up by default anymore, so you’ll have to go find them. If you hire, making room for beginners is now something you have to choose on purpose.
items.summary_html:
The grunt work that taught me how to do my job is the same work Anthropic says its teams can now hand to Claude.

Anthropic studied its own hiring. The junior share of its technical hires fell from 27% to 9%, and that happened while the company kept hiring. The teams that use Claude most said a lot of coding and bug finding can move to the AI. When interviewers wrote up candidates, comments about judgment and working independently grew more than anything else.

When I started at Scouts, I had very little to show for myself. For the first year, I mostly wrote code, put together slide decks, did basic analysis, and tried to build trust with our clients. None of it felt like training at the time. Looking back, that year is where I learned what clients care about and how to explain a finding so someone believes it. The judgment companies now screen for came out of that work. I didn’t walk in with it.

I’m not directly on the hiring side, but over the last five years I’ve helped sports teams interview and hire a fair amount. I understand the pull. If AI can handle the first draft, it makes sense to hire people who already know what to do with it. I just don’t know who trains the next group if every organization makes that call.

One caveat: this is one company studying itself, and it sells the tool, so it may not predict what every employer does. Still, it’s worth paying attention to.

If you’re early in your career, the reps that used to come with a first job won’t show up by default anymore, so you’ll have to go find them. If you hire, making room for beginners is now something you have to choose on purpose.

items.title: Please Stop Telling Your AI to “Search Harder”
items.summary: Humans used to give infrastructure a breather. AI agents don’t. In this episode of Debug Mode, Erika and Demetrios explore what happens when one person’s prompt triggers a burst of searches, API calls, and compute-intensive requests - and why existing services, gateways, and pricing models can struggle to keep up. They unpack the differences between microservices and agent workloads, revisit SaaS multi-tenancy, and explore Agent Substrate’s approach to actors, shared workers, sandboxes, and suspend-and-resume operations. Along the way: cold starts, context persistence, a Spotify detour, and a practical question for anyone building with agents - do you actually need this infrastructure, or will it become another invisible layer inside the products you use? items.title: AI Simulation Is One Point From Human Parity
items.summary: Simile's agents predict people's behavior with 85%+ accuracy. And 85 is much closer to the ceiling than it sounds. Ask people the same question twice and their answers change 13 to 14% of the time. Humans don't fully agree with themselves, so the ceiling on predicting them is 86 to 89%. Joon Sung Park, Co-founder & CEO of Simile, explains to Lukas Biewald what 85% accuracy actually means, and why it's approaching parity with human subjects.

items.title: Cybersecurity for the Agentic AI Era (Ep.1040 with Amy Blackshaw)
items.summary: In Episode #1040, Amy Blackshaw (SVP at Palo Alto Networks) joins @JonKrohnLearns to explain what changes about cybersecurity when attackers can think for free. Nearly every breach, Amy argues, comes down to someone getting hold of an identity they should not have had, and frontier AI has not created new attack techniques so much as deleted the cost of the expert reasoning that used to chain them together. The recent Hugging Face intrusion is her case in point: agents sustained an action every 20 seconds for four and a half days, but what let them reach the crown jewels was ordinary privilege hygiene. In this episode, she explains why the line between privileged and ordinary users has dissolved, what makes an agentic identity unlike either a human or a service account, and what she wants every organisation to do first. In this episode you will learn: • (00:00:00) Introduction • (02:26) What identity security actually means • (05:09) Why AI changed the economics, not the attacks • (07:41) What really went wrong in the Hugging Face breach • (19:26) Why agentic identities are unlike anything before them Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1040

items.title: What $200B in Exposed Tech Revenue Means for Indian Workers
items.summary: For two decades, the Indian IT sector operated on a simple deal: clients paid for engineers by the month, and firms supplied the headcount. But what happens when the month suddenly needs fewer engineers? Billing by the hour works beautifully, until the hour gets shorter. A new BCG India report warns that roughly $200 billion of existing IT services revenue is now exposed to contraction as AI agents take over routine coding, testing, and processes. While massive firms like TCS are pivoting to deploy "forward-deployed AI engineers," the shift from billing by the hour to paying for outcomes could fundamentally alter the delivery pyramid that Indian IT is built on. But it's not all doom and gloom—BCG also projects that $100 to $200 billion in new work will be on the table by 2030 for the firms that can adapt. In this episode of Front Page, we sit down with Sreyssha George, Managing Director and Partner at BCG in Bengaluru, to break down the harsh realities of the new tech landscape. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 📌 Note: The video thumbnail is for representational purposes and was created with the assistance of AI. 📩 For inquiries or questions, contact us at: info@aimmediahouse.com ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 📌 ABOUT FRONT PAGE Front Page is a daily live news briefing covering AI, enterprise tech, semiconductors, and India’s role in the global technology economy.
